cases.reviewerAnswer: Poder + infinitive expresses possibility or ability: Hoy no puedo salir. No intervening preposition is required.
Saber + infinitive expresses learned know-how: Sé nadar. Poder can also express ability.
cases.element: content.body.scope.noteUk: "Додатковий крок, щоб значення poder не поширювалося на навички."
cases.defect: This categorically excludes skills from the meaning of poder. Poder can express a person's capacity to perform an activity; the distinction from saber is not an absolute prohibition.
cases.correction: Explain that saber explicitly expresses learned know-how, while poder expresses ability or possibility. Use sufficiently explicit contexts when assessing the distinction.
sources: RAE/ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española, entries «poder» and «saber», ability-related senses (from memory).
cases.notes: The construction, examples and main rule are otherwise correct.

cases.reviewerAnswer: Tengo que estudiar expresses necessity; puedo estudiar, possibility; quiero estudiar, desire; voy a estudiar, intention or a plan.
Sé conducir, pero hoy no puedo: no tengo coche.
cases.notes: The example clearly establishes know-how versus a present circumstantial limitation. The variant policy appropriately requires clarification when context does not establish that contrast.

cases.reviewerAnswer: Tener que + infinitive expresses necessity or obligation: Tengo que trabajar. Que is required.
Present-tense acabar de + infinitive expresses a recent event: Acabo de llegar.
Empezar a + infinitive expresses beginning an activity: Empiezo a trabajar a las nueve.
Volver a + infinitive expresses repetition: Vuelvo a leer el texto. Volver a casa expresses returning home.
Acabar means to finish or end; acabar de + infinitive can express having just done something.
Llamar means to call, including by telephone: Te llamo luego.
Expected frames: poder/saber + infinitive; tener que + infinitive; acabar de, empezar a and volver a + infinitive.

cases.reviewerAnswer: a (puedo) is the likely intended answer; b (sé) also fits if not owning a car explains never learning to drive.
cases.element: task.prompt[1].text: "No ___ conducir: no tengo coche."; task.options[1] marks "sé" incorrect.
cases.defect: The sentence does not establish whether the speaker knows how to drive. Car ownership can explain either a current practical limitation or why the speaker has never learned. The feedback assumes the first reading.
cases.correction: Establish explicitly that the speaker knows how to drive but currently lacks access to a car, or allow both readings.
sources: Course contract rule 2 and the supplied definition of the verdict "uncertain".

cases.reviewerAnswer: a (sabe) is the expected know-how reading; b (puede) can express the child's inability to read.
cases.element: task.prompt[1].text: "Mi hija tiene tres años y no ___ leer."; task.options[1] marks "puede" incorrect.
cases.defect: Age alone does not uniquely select saber. No sabe leer describes missing learned know-how; no puede leer can describe lack of reading capacity. Poder is not grammatically excluded merely because reading is learned.
cases.correction: Specify that the learner must express "does not know how to read", or accept both interpretations with differentiated explanations.
sources: Course contract rule 2 and the supplied definition of the verdict "uncertain".
RAE/ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española, entries «poder» and «saber», ability-related senses (from memory).
